questions.explain: A has 2 rows (2 inner lists) and 3 columns (3 numbers in each row), so A.shape is (2, 3).

questions.explain: x[1:4] takes positions 1, 2 and 3 (it stops before 4): [20 30 40].

questions.code:
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * b)
questions.hint: The * sign works position by position: first with first, second with second …
questions.explain: * is element-wise: 1×10, 2×20, 3×30 = [10 40 90]. (140 would be the dot product.)

questions.code:
a = np.array([2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5])
print(np.dot(a, b))
questions.hint: A dot product has two steps. Step 1 is the same as a * b. Step 2 turns the result into ONE number.
questions.explain: Multiply the pairs (2×4 = 8, 3×5 = 15), then add them: 8 + 15 = 23.

questions.q: What is the difference between * and @ in NumPy?
options: @ works only with single numbers; * works only with arrays
* is matrix multiplication; @ multiplies position by position
There is no difference; @ is only a shorter way to write *
* multiplies position by position; @ is matrix multiplication
questions.hint: Remember the memory trick slide. One sign matches positions, the other combines rows with columns.
questions.explain: * = element-wise (match positions). @ = matrix multiplication (each result is a row × column dot product).

questions.q: A.shape is (2, 3) and B.shape is (3, 4). What is the shape of A @ B?
options: Error: shapes do not match
questions.hint: Write the shapes next to each other: (2, 3) @ (3, 4). The inside numbers must match. Which numbers are left?
questions.explain: (m, n) @ (n, p) → (m, p). Inside: 3 = 3, so it works. Outside numbers give the result: (2, 4).

questions.q: Which matrix multiplication gives an ERROR?
questions.hint: For each option, look only at the two numbers in the middle. Every number in a row needs a partner in the column.
questions.explain: (2, 3) @ (2, 4) fails because the inside numbers are 3 and 2. 3 ≠ 2, so rows and columns have different lengths.

options: Error: shapes do not match
questions.hint: NumPy “stretches” one single number so it fits the whole array.
questions.explain: Broadcasting: NumPy uses 10 for every position. [1+10, 2+10, 3+10] = [11 12 13].

questions.q: A.shape is (3, 4). Which array can NOT be added to A?
options: An array with shape (1, 4)
An array with shape (2,)
An array with shape (4,)
An array with shape (3, 1)
questions.hint: Read shapes from RIGHT to LEFT. Two sizes work together if they are equal, or if one of them is 1.
questions.explain: (3, 4) + (2,): the last sizes are 4 and 2. They are not equal and neither is 1, so it is an error. The other three all work.

questions.hint: axis=0 means move DOWN. You get one answer for every column.
questions.explain: axis=0 collapses the rows: 1+4 = 5, 2+5 = 7, 3+6 = 9 → [5 7 9]. axis=1 would give [6 15].

questions.code:
x = np.array([10, 12, 14, 16, 18])
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
print(z[2])
questions.hint: First find x.mean(). Then look at x[2]. What happens in the top part of the formula?
questions.explain: x.mean() = 14 and x[2] = 14. 14 − 14 = 0, and 0 divided by anything is 0.

options: Error: data was used
questions.hint: Ask the key question from class: is data on the LEFT side of the = sign?
questions.explain: data * 2 makes a NEW result, stored in new_data. data itself is not changed: [1 2 3].

questions.hint: np.delete builds something new. Did we keep it with an = sign?
questions.explain: np.delete returns a NEW array, but we did not save it. data is still [10 20 30 40]. To keep it: data = np.delete(data, 1).

questions.hint: Two steps: first NumPy asks the question for every value, then the [ ] keeps some values.

questions.code:
data = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
part = data[1:3]
part[0] = 999
print(data)
options: Error: part is read-only
questions.hint: Remember the warning slide about views and copies. Is part a new box, or a window to the same numbers?
questions.explain: A slice is a view: part looks at the SAME numbers as data. Changing part[0] also changes data[1]. Use .copy() to avoid this.

questions.q: You loaded students.csv into data and changed some values in data. What happens to students.csv?
options: Nothing changes until you save with np.savetxt(...)
It updates automatically when the value changes
It is deleted, because data is now different
It updates automatically when Python closes
questions.hint: Think about the photocopy example. Where does data live — on the disk or in memory (RAM)?
questions.explain: data is a copy in memory. The file on disk changes only when you save, e.g. np.savetxt(...).

questions.hint: The T stands for transpose. What does a transpose do to rows and columns?
questions.explain: Transpose swaps rows and columns: (2, 3) becomes (3, 2).

questions.q: A neural-network layer: what is Y.shape?
questions.code:
X.shape  # (32, 10)  → 32 samples, 10 features
W.shape  # (10, 4)
b.shape  # (4,)
Y = X @ W + b
questions.hint: Do it in two steps. First use the shape rule for X @ W. Then ask: does + b change the shape?
questions.explain: (32, 10) @ (10, 4) → (32, 4). b with shape (4,) is broadcast to every row, so Y stays (32, 4).
